title: When Rates Drop, Your Servicing Portfolio Gets Called by Someone: Refinance Recapture With an AI Voice Agent, and the Tests That Decide Who It Calls
summary: A rate move puts thousands of loans in the money in the same week, and the servicer has the data to reach those borrowers first. Before an AI agent dials any of them, it has to know which loans can actually close: VA's seasoning and recoupment tests under 38 U.S.C. 3709, the early payoff window on loans you sold, which consent covers a marketing call, and what the agent may and may not say about savings. What we learned running a voice agent on a lender's funnel, applied to the recapture campaign.
body_markdown:
## Who This Is For


Heads of consumer-direct lending and portfolio retention at lenders that keep servicing, Directors of Mortgage Ops who staff the surge, and Chief Compliance Officers who have to approve an outbound campaign to the lender's own borrowers before the rate window closes.


## The Week Rates Move


Every servicer that has been through a rate drop knows the pattern. Overnight, a large slice of the portfolio is in the money. Trigger leads go out to competitors as soon as borrowers start shopping, which we wrote about in our post on[trigger leads and the Homebuyers Privacy Protection Act](https://www.seiright.com/blog/trigger-leads-homebuyers-privacy-protection-act-ai-mortgage-outreach) . The servicer has the best information in the market: the note rate, the balance, the payment history, the phone number, and a relationship. It also has a retention team sized for a normal month.


So the recapture campaign is a speed problem, and the obvious answer is an agent that can call everyone. That is where the[Loan Officer Assistant](https://www.seiright.com/for-lenders/loan-officer-assistant) comes in, and it is the same agent we ran for a[top-25 independent mortgage bank in California](https://www.seiright.com/case-study/sei-x-ca-mortgage-lender) , where appointments booked with loan officers rose 9.2 times on average and lead-to-funded conversion rose 12%. The lesson from that deployment that matters most here was a side effect: several loan officers had to block hours out of their own calendars because the agent booked them faster than they could take the calls. In a recapture surge that happens in the first afternoon, so booking caps per loan officer, and licensing by state, are settings the lender controls before the campaign starts.


The harder question in recapture is whom to call at all, because a meaningful share of the in-the-money list cannot, or should not, close a refinance yet.


## VA Loans Have a Statutory Clock and a Benefit Test


For VA loans, Congress wrote the rules into the statute after a wave of serial refinancing. Under[38 U.S.C. 3709](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/38/3709) , VA cannot guarantee an interest rate reduction refinance unless three things are true.


The first is seasoning. The new loan cannot close until the later of two dates: the date the borrower has made six consecutive monthly payments on the loan being refinanced, and 210 days after the first payment due date of that loan. The second is recoupment. The fees, closing costs and expenses of the refinance, other than taxes, escrow and the VA funding fee, have to be recouped through lower monthly payments within 36 months. The third is a net tangible benefit, which VA's regulation sets as a minimum rate reduction, half a percentage point for a fixed-to-fixed refinance, with a larger reduction required for a fixed-to-adjustable move. FHA's streamline refinance has its own seasoning and net tangible benefit tests in Handbook 4000.1, and Ginnie Mae applies a seasoning requirement of its own to the refinance loans it will pool.


The practical consequence for a campaign is that a VA loan closed five months ago is in the money and cannot be refinanced into a VA loan yet. Calling that veteran today produces either an application that cannot close or a conversation about a non-VA product that may be worse for them, and both are close to the pattern the statute was written to stop. So the agent's call list is built from the[Loan Graph](https://www.seiright.com/platform/loan-graph) with the seasoning test applied against a projected closing date, not today's date, because a refinance started now closes in weeks. A loan that fails seasoning gets scheduled instead of dropped: the agent holds a goal for that loan and wakes on the date the test will pass, minus the lender's typical time to close, which is the long-horizon behavior that lets the campaign continue for months without anyone rebuilding a list.


Recoupment cannot be confirmed until a loan officer prices the loan, so the agent does not try. It screens out loans where no plausible rate would clear the benefit test, and it leaves the actual test to the LOS pricing and the loan officer, with the result recorded in the file.


## Loans You Sold Recently Carry an Early Payoff Cost


The second filter is commercial, and it is the one most often missed. Most investors and aggregators require the originating lender to refund some or all of the premium if a loan pays off within a set early window after sale. Soliciting a borrower whose loan you delivered four months ago can cost you the premium you were paid for it. Our post on[early payment default and early payoff](https://www.seiright.com/blog/early-payment-default-early-payoff-qc-feedback-loop-ai-mortgage-repurchase) covers how these windows feed back into QC. For the campaign, the purchase agreement's early payoff terms go into the[Rulebook](https://www.seiright.com/how-it-works#rulebook) per investor, and a loan inside its window is held out of the list or scheduled for the day the window closes, with the lender deciding which.


## A Marketing Call Needs Marketing Consent


The servicer has the borrower's phone number because the borrower gave it to the servicer. That supports servicing calls. A call to offer a refinance is telemarketing, and the TCPA rules for it are stricter. Under the FCC's rules at[47 CFR 64.1200](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-47/section-64.1200) , a telemarketing call to a cell phone using an artificial or prerecorded voice needs prior express written consent, and the FCC confirmed in 2024 that AI-generated voices count as artificial. We covered the consent questions in detail in our post on[speed-to-lead and TCPA](https://www.seiright.com/blog/mortgage-speed-to-lead-ai-voice-agent-tcpa-calling-hours-safe-act-fair-lending) . The recapture version of the problem is that servicing consent and marketing consent are different records, and in many servicing files only the first one exists.


So the agent keeps them separate and checks the marketing record before every outbound refinance call. A borrower with no written marketing consent is not called by the agent. They can be reached in other ways the lender's counsel approves: a message inside the servicing portal, a mailed notice, or an inbound line the agent answers when the borrower calls. A borrower who says "stop calling me about refinancing" has revoked marketing consent, and the FCC's revocation rules, in force since April 2025, require honoring a revocation made by any reasonable means within ten business days. Whether that revocation also reaches servicing calls is a question the lender's counsel answers once, and the Rulebook carries the answer so every call applies it the same way.


There is a data question too. If the servicer and the lender making the new loan are separate affiliated companies, Regulation V's affiliate marketing rule at[12 CFR 1022.21](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1022/21/) can require an opt-out notice before servicing information is used to solicit, subject to its exceptions. Which entity is making the call is a fact the campaign has to get right before the first dial.


## What the Agent Says About Savings, and What It Does Not


In 2020 the CFPB ran a sweep of lenders that mailed deceptive advertisements for VA refinances, and it ended in nine consent orders carrying over $4.4 million in penalties; the[Go Direct Lenders order](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/policy-compliance/enforcement/actions/go-direct-lenders-inc/) is a representative one, with mailers that described an adjustable-rate loan as fixed and misstated credit terms. The orders cited the CFPA's deception standard, the Mortgage Acts and Practices Advertising Rule and Regulation Z. An outbound call is advertising too.[Regulation Z 1026.24](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1026/24/) governs what a stated rate or payment triggers, and our post on[AI-generated mortgage advertising and the MAP Rule](https://www.seiright.com/blog/ai-generated-mortgage-advertising-map-rule-regulation-n-reg-z-1026-24) goes through those triggers.


So the agent's script is narrow by design. It tells the borrower that rates have moved, that their loan may be a candidate for a refinance, and that a licensed loan officer can tell them whether a refinance would lower their payment and how long the costs would take to recover. It does not quote a rate, a payment or a savings figure, and it does not say the borrower will qualify, which also keeps it on the right side of the[SAFE Act licensing line](https://www.seiright.com/blog/safe-act-ai-mortgage-assistants-nmls-licensing-line) . Borrowers ask "how much would I save," and the agent's answer is the appointment. Every call is scored against that boundary, the same way the[Compliance Agent](https://www.seiright.com/for-lenders/compliance-agent) scores a loan officer's calls, so drift toward a number gets caught on the call where it happened.


## Who Gets Called Is a Fair Lending Question


A recapture list is a marketing decision about which borrowers hear about a cheaper loan first. If the in-the-money screen, the loan-size floor or the geographic priority correlates with race or national origin, the lender has built a disparate-impact problem into the list before anyone has picked up the phone.[Regulation B at 12 CFR 1002.4(b)](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-policy/regulations/1002/4/) prohibits discouraging prospective applicants on a prohibited basis, and marketing selection has been part of the redlining matters regulators have brought. So we report the composition of each campaign list against the portfolio it was drawn from, by census tract characteristics, before the campaign runs and as it runs, and a skew goes to the fair-lending officer with the filter that caused it. The screen criteria themselves are written down and versioned, so the lender can show what the list was built from on the day it was built. More on this in our post on[fair lending and AI agents](https://www.seiright.com/blog/fair-lending-disparate-impact-ai-agents-ecoa-hmda) .


## What the Campaign Looks Like When It Works


The list is every in-the-money loan in the portfolio, filtered by the VA and FHA seasoning tests at a projected closing date, the investor early payoff windows, marketing consent and the benefit screen. The loans that fail a timing test are scheduled rather than dropped. The agent calls the rest inside calling hours, books licensed loan officers within the caps the lender set, answers the inbound calls the portal message and the mailer produce, and records every consent it relied on and every borrower who said stop. The loan officer takes the appointment with the screen results in front of them and runs the real recoupment and benefit tests in pricing.


That last step stays with people because it is where the borrower decides whether the refinance is worth it, and the statute's benefit test exists so that decision is made on real numbers. The agent's job is to make sure the right borrowers reach that conversation first, and that the ones who cannot benefit yet are called on the day they can.
